This has implications for the whole world. Middle-income countries are home to three
            out of every four people—and nearly two-thirds of those who struggle in extreme poverty.
          They are responsible for 40 percent of the world’s total economic output—and nearly two-
             thirds of global carbon emissions. In short, the global effort to end extreme poverty and
            spread prosperity and livability will largely be won or lost in these countries.
            The road ahead has even stiffer challenges than those seen in the past: rapidly aging
            populations and burgeoning debt, fierce geopolitical and trade frictions, and the growing
               difficulty of speeding up economic progress without fouling the environment. Yet many
           middle-income countries still use a playbook from the last century, relying mainly on pol­
               icies designed to expand investment. That is like driving a car just in first gear and trying
             to make it go faster. If they stick with the old playbook, most developing countries will lose
            the race to create reasonably prosperous societies by the middle of this century. At current
             trends, it will take China more than 10 years just to reach one-quarter of US income per
              capita, Indonesia nearly 70 years, and India 75 years.
            The team that has written this report hopes to radically alter this arithmetic. Our hope
                 is that World Development Report 2024 will, in short order, make the expression “middle-
           income trap” completely obsolete.

Figure 1.5
Growth is expected to slow down as countries approach the economic frontier (United States). Scatter/line chart with x-axis: "GDP per capita relative to the frontier (United States) (%)" from 0 to 100, and y-axis: "Annual growth in GDP per capita (%)" from 0 to 7. The figure shows multiple country trajectories connecting projected recent-history points, with a legend for Argentina, Bangladesh, Bulgaria, Chile, China, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Poland, and Türkiye. Solid lines indicate countries that will experience convergence to the frontier over 2023–2100; dashed lines indicate countries that will experience divergence from the frontier over 2023–2100, although they were closer to the frontier in 2022. Visible patterns: Poland is a long solid teal line extending from roughly the mid-20s percent of US GDP per capita to 100%, with growth easing from a little above 5% to about 3.3–3.8%; China is a solid orange-red line extending from roughly the low-20s to the low-60s, with growth around 5% falling to around 2–3%; India is a solid brown/orange line around the low single digits to the mid-20s, flattening near 3.8%; Bangladesh is a solid olive line from very low frontier proximity to the high-20s, falling from above 6% toward about 3%; Indonesia is a solid blue line from the high single digits to the high-20s, settling near 3%; Türkiye is a solid gray line from the mid-20s to low-30s, near 2%; Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Bulgaria are dashed trajectories rising from low frontier proximity into the mid-teens to low-20s while growth rises sharply from near 0–1% to around 1.5–3%. Source: WDR 2024 team. Note: Projections are based on extrapolation of recent historical trends using the World Bank’s Long Term Growth Model. GDP = gross domestic product.

This has implications for the whole world. Middle-income countries are home to three
            out of every four people—and nearly two-thirds of those who struggle in extreme poverty.
          They are responsible for 40 percent of the world’s total economic output—and nearly two-
             thirds of global carbon emissions. In short, the global effort to end extreme poverty and
            spread prosperity and livability will largely be won or lost in these countries.
            The road ahead has even stiffer challenges than those seen in the past: rapidly aging
            populations and burgeoning debt, fierce geopolitical and trade frictions, and the growing
               difficulty of speeding up economic progress without fouling the environment. Yet many
           middle-income countries still use a playbook from the last century, relying mainly on pol­
               icies designed to expand investment. That is like driving a car just in first gear and trying
             to make it go faster. If they stick with the old playbook, most developing countries will lose
            the race to create reasonably prosperous societies by the middle of this century. At current
             trends, it will take China more than 10 years just to reach one-quarter of US income per
              capita, Indonesia nearly 70 years, and India 75 years.
            The team that has written this report hopes to radically alter this arithmetic. Our hope
                 is that World Development Report 2024 will, in short order, make the expression “middle-
           income trap” completely obsolete.

Figure 1.5
Growth is expected to slow down as countries approach the economic frontier (United States). Scatter/line chart with x-axis: "GDP per capita relative to the frontier (United States) (%)" from 0 to 100, and y-axis: "Annual growth in GDP per capita (%)" from 0 to 7. The figure shows multiple country trajectories connecting projected recent-history points, with a legend for Argentina, Bangladesh, Bulgaria, Chile, China, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Poland, and Türkiye. Solid lines indicate countries that will experience convergence to the frontier over 2023–2100; dashed lines indicate countries that will experience divergence from the frontier over 2023–2100, although they were closer to the frontier in 2022. Visible patterns: Poland is a long solid teal line extending from roughly the mid-20s percent of US GDP per capita to 100%, with growth easing from a little above 5% to about 3.3–3.8%; China is a solid orange-red line extending from roughly the low-20s to the low-60s, with growth around 5% falling to around 2–3%; India is a solid brown/orange line around the low single digits to the mid-20s, flattening near 3.8%; Bangladesh is a solid olive line from very low frontier proximity to the high-20s, falling from above 6% toward about 3%; Indonesia is a solid blue line from the high single digits to the high-20s, settling near 3%; Türkiye is a solid gray line from the mid-20s to low-30s, near 2%; Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Bulgaria are dashed trajectories rising from low frontier proximity into the mid-teens to low-20s while growth rises sharply from near 0–1% to around 1.5–3%. Source: WDR 2024 team. Note: Projections are based on extrapolation of recent historical trends using the World Bank’s Long Term Growth Model. GDP = gross domestic product.
